content: Uranium-238 (U-238) is the most abundant isotope of uranium found in nature. When it absorbs a neutron, it transforms into uranium-239 (U-239), an unstable isotope. U-239 undergoes beta decay to form neptunium-239 (Np-239), which subsequently decays into plutonium-239 (Pu-239) with a half-life of 2.355 days. Approximately 99.284% of natural uranium consists of U-238, which has an extraordinarily long half-life of 4.46 billion years (1.41 × 10^17 seconds). Depleted uranium primarily contains U-238, while enriched uranium has a higher concentration of the fissile isotope uranium-235 (U-235). Reprocessed uranium is also predominantly U-238 but includes significant amounts of uranium-236 (U-236) and other isotopes ranging from uranium-232 to uranium-238, excluding uranium-237. In nuclear reactors, U-238 can be converted into Pu-239, which serves as a fissile material for nuclear weapons or as a reactor fuel. In fact, in standard nuclear reactors, up to one-third of the energy produced comes from the fission of Pu-239, which is generated in situ from U-238 rather than being supplied as an initial fuel. U-238 itself is not directly usable as a nuclear fuel. However, breeder reactors are designed to transmute fertile isotopes like U-238 into fissile isotopes such as Pu-239. Estimates suggest that the global supply of U-238 could sustain breeder reactors for anywhere between 10,000 years and five billion years. Breeder reactor technology has been implemented in several facilities. As of December 2005, the BN-600 reactor at the Beloyarsk Nuclear Power Station in Russia was the only operational breeder reactor producing power. Russia has plans to construct another breeder reactor, the BN-800, at the same site. Japan's Monju breeder reactor is also slated for restart after being inactive since 1995. Additionally, both China and India have announced plans to develop breeder reactors. A conceptual design known as the Clean And Environmentally Safe Advanced Reactor (CAESAR) aims to use steam as a moderator to control delayed neutrons, potentially enabling the use of U-238 as a fuel once the reactor is initiated with low-enriched uranium (LEU). However, this design remains in the early stages of development. U-238 is also employed as a material for radiation shielding. Its alpha radiation is easily contained by a non-radioactive casing, and its high atomic weight and electron density make it highly effective at absorbing gamma rays and X-rays. However, it is less effective than water at stopping fast neutrons. Both metallic depleted uranium and depleted uranium dioxide are used in radiation shielding applications. U-238 is approximately five times more effective than lead at shielding gamma rays, allowing for thinner shielding layers with equivalent protective capacity. DUCRETE, a type of concrete that incorporates uranium dioxide aggregate instead of traditional gravel, is being explored as a material for dry cask storage systems to contain radioactive waste. The process of downblending involves diluting highly enriched uranium (HEU) with depleted or natural uranium to produce low-enriched uranium (LEU), which is suitable for use in commercial nuclear reactors. U-238 from depleted or natural uranium is also combined with recycled plutonium from dismantled nuclear weapons to create mixed oxide (MOX) fuel, which is repurposed for reactor use. In modern nuclear weapons, U-238 is often used as a tamper material. The tamper surrounds the fissile core, reflecting neutrons and adding inertia to the implosion of the plutonium charge. This increases the weapon's efficiency and reduces the amount of fissile material required. In thermonuclear weapons, U-238 can encase the fusion fuel. The high-energy neutrons produced during the fusion reaction induce fission in the U-238, significantly increasing the weapon's explosive yield. Such designs are referred to as fission-fusion-fission weapons, as they involve three sequential stages of energy release. For example, in the 1952 Ivy Mike thermonuclear test, 77% of the 10.4-megaton yield was derived from the fast fission of the depleted uranium tamper. Because depleted uranium does not have a critical mass, it can be added to thermonuclear weapons in virtually unlimited quantities. The 1961 Soviet Tsar Bomba test, which yielded 50 megatons, achieved this output primarily through fusion, as the U-238 stage was replaced with lead to reduce fallout. Had U-238 been used, the yield could have reached 100 megatons, producing fallout equivalent to one-third of the global total at that time. The decay of U-238 produces thorium-234 (Th-234), which has a half-life of 246,000 years. This property makes it useful for dating sediments that are between 100,000 and 1,200,000 years old. The mean lifetime of U-238 is approximately 2 × 10^17 seconds, and one mole of U-238 emits 3 × 10^6 alpha particles per second, generating an equivalent number of Th-234 atoms. In a closed system, equilibrium is reached where all intermediate decay products, except for the stable end product lead-206 (Pb-206), exist in fixed ratios. Over time, the amount of Pb-206 increases as U-238 decreases. In equilibrium, the decay rate of U-238 is matched by the production rate of its decay products. For example, in one mole of U-238, there are 9 × 10^12 atoms of Th-234 at equilibrium, corresponding to 1.5 × 10^-11 moles. The energy released during the first three steps of the U-238 decay chain is approximately 6.7 MeV per decay, resulting in a power output of 3 µW per mole of U-238. Over the isotope's mean lifetime, this energy release totals approximately 600 GJ.
